raw_response.headline_result_summary: Using a modified difference-in-differences design across 3,182 rural Peruvian households (exploiting village-level rollout of the PETT land-titling program interacted with lack of pre-program property title), Meeks (2018) finds that rural land titling leads to a statistically significant 5.9 percentage point increase in household access to an improved water source (coef = 0.059, SE = 0.027, p < 0.05; baseline untitled mean = 76.6%) and a 15.1 percentage point increase in household toilet/public sanitation or septic access (coef = 0.151, SE = 0.0347, p < 0.01; baseline untitled mean = 35.7%). Reliance on river water falls by a borderline-significant 4.3 percentage points (SE = 0.024, p < 0.10), while tanker truck/vendor reliance is unchanged (SE = 0.009). Mechanism regressions show recent connections to public water networks (+3.2 pp, SE = 0.019, p < 0.10) and public sanitation networks (+15.1 pp, SE = 0.035, p < 0.01), with significant household out-of-pocket financing only for sanitation (+2.4 pp, SE = 0.009, p < 0.01) and null effects on household water connection expenditure, credit use, and monthly water payments.
raw_response.specification_or_coding_pitfalls: 1. Stripped minus glyphs in Elsevier PDF text layer: Plain-text extraction omits Unicode minus signs in Tables 4, 5, 6, and 7 (as well as operator symbols in Eq. 1). Specifically, River water coefficients in Table 4 (-0.078***, -0.070***) and Table 5 (-0.043* on program * no prior) are negative (confirmed by Table 3 means—0.077 for PETT title vs. 0.192 for No title—and p. 9 text stating 'decreases in river water use as household sources come with the PETT program'), main-effect 'no prior title' rows in Tables 5-6 reflect lower baseline access among untitled households, and Table 7 Columns 5-6 (-0.110***, -0.067**) are negative (confirmed by p. 11 text: 'program households signiﬁcantly less likely to report a need for these services'). A careless reader relying only on stripped table text without reading the prose and descriptive means would invert these signs. 2. Polarity reversal on unimproved water sources and unmet community need: Higher values of River and Tanker truck/vendor (Tables 4-5) and perceived need for future public networks (Table 7) represent WORSE access/greater unmet need, whereas Improved water source and Sanitation represent BETTER access. 3. Borderline p < 0.10 vs. p < 0.05 significance: Improved water source (0.059**, p < 0.05) and Sanitation (0.151***, p < 0.01) pass conventional 5% significance in the preferred DD (Table 5), whereas the DD reduction in River water (-0.043*, SE = 0.024) and the DD increase in 5-year public water network connection (0.032*, SE = 0.019, Table 6 Panel A Col 1) are only significant at the 10% level. 4. Non-causal cross-sectional marginal effects vs. preferred DD on sanitation: Naive cross-sectional marginal effects (Table 4 Col 4) show a null coefficient for PETT title on sanitation (0.016, SE = 0.025), whereas the preferred modified DD (Table 5 Col 4) finds a large positive effect (0.151***, SE = 0.0347).
raw_response.study_design: Quasi-experimental modified difference-in-differences (exploiting spatial variation in phased-in village rollout of the PETT land-titling program interacted with pre-program household title status, with region fixed effects and household controls; verified with propensity score matching DD) using cross-sectional 2004 rural household survey data
raw_response.unit_and_sample_size: Rural households in Peru (2004 Land Titling Special Project Survey); total survey N = 3,204 households (648 PETT title, 1,076 other title, 1,480 no title; Tables 1-3); regression analytic sample N = 3,182 households (Tables 4-7)
